summary:
Slovakia poses no entry or documentation obstacle specific to a trans visitor. Legal gender recognition has been available for more than four decades, and no law restricts which toilets a person may use. Entry and residence fall under the free-movement rules of the European Union, and the Court of Justice of the European Union's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018 required the Slovak Interior Ministry to recognise the residence rights of same-sex couples married elsewhere in the union.

The recognition procedure itself is medicalised and restrictive. In force rules require surgical sterilisation before identity documents can be amended, registry offices are refusing to process gender-change applications pending new standards, and a Ministry of Health guideline that had permitted document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of government coalition stability. A bill of 24 February 2023 would narrow recognition further to people whose sex was wrongly assigned at birth provable only by a karyotype test; it passed first reading with 87 votes, and the sources do not record its subsequent fate.

Legislative attempts to abolish legal gender recognition have so far failed. Bills tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021 and again on 13 January 2023 sought to ban legal gender change, with the 2023 version also outlawing medical transition and carrying a prison sentence of at least four years; all failed, mostly through abstentions. In an April 2023 letter to the Slovak National Council, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović reported no discernible progress six months after the Tepláreň attack, judged the human rights of LGBTI people to be more at risk rather than less, and raised specific concern about regressive legislative proposals including a ban on legal gender recognition.

Trans-specific healthcare has been unstable. The Ministry of Health's standards of care were revoked on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and MPs, after which no valid standards existed; by 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care and individuals were being forced to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries remains to be seen.

The security climate is the material concern. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger arrived in Bratislava at about 18:35, and at 19:11 fired eight shots at the LGBT bar Teplaren, killing two people and injuring one; the bar was his stated fallback target. The perpetrator died and the incident is treated as the country's first modern terrorist attack, met with terrorism charges and official condemnation. A 7 February 2023 assessment reports that rights groups regard the attack as having marked a new era for trans people in Slovakia, with the community's situation remaining precarious and fears about the future having intensified afterwards.

Protection machinery exists in part. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services, and applies to the armed forces, where LGBT people serve openly. A Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis; the sources do not state that gender identity was added to that provision.

Any change of legal gender invalidates an existing marriage, and Slovakia recognises neither civil unions nor same-sex marriage, so a visitor in a same-sex partnership should not expect that relationship to be acknowledged. Hostile rhetoric from senior officials is documented: on 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, publicly claimed that Europe is dying because of an excessive number of LGBT people.
